Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Carlos Hernandez still remembers the acrid taste of smoke and sweat that lingered in his mouth for days after the ambush. It was 1972, and he was a young soldier serving in Vietnam. His unit had been patrolling through a dense jungle when they were caught off guard by enemy fire. The chaos and confusion that followed are etched in his memory like scars. Carlos can recall the sound of gunfire and screams, the feeling of weightlessness as he fell to the ground, and the sensation of dizziness that washed over him as he struggled to get back up. Decades later, that same taste would transport Carlos back to those moments. He couldn't quite explain why, but whenever he encountered a specific type of cigar smoke or even certain types of spices, his stomach would drop, and he'd feel lightheaded. At first, it was just an occasional annoyance, something he learned to avoid by steering clear of certain situations or places. But over time, the association grew stronger, until the mere whiff of that smell could send him spiraling. Talking about the event itself wasn't much better. Carlos would often find himself glossing over details or changing the subject when asked about his time in Vietnam. He'd tried to explain it to friends and family before, but the words always seemed to get stuck in his throat. It was as if the memories themselves were too heavy to be spoken aloud. As a special education teacher, Carlos had learned to navigate complex emotions and challenging situations with ease. But he couldn't shake the feeling that certain environments or conversations might trigger those same feelings of overwhelm. He began to avoid situations that made him feel strong emotions – whether it was a heated discussion with colleagues or a particularly moving lesson plan. It wasn't that he didn't care; it's just that he'd come to believe that his own emotional well-being depended on maintaining a certain level of detachment. At school, Carlos developed the habit of sitting near exits and constantly scanning the room for signs of potential threats. His students might have seen him as vigilant or even overprotective, but for Carlos, these habits provided a sense of comfort in an uncertain world. He'd often find himself mentally mapping out escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere – whether it was a new classroom or a social gathering. Sounds, too, had become a source of hypervigilance for Carlos. Loud noises would make him jump; unexpected sounds would leave him on edge. His friends might tease him about being jumpy, but Carlos couldn't help the way his body responded to those stimuli. It was as if he'd developed an extra layer of skin that allowed him to sense even the smallest changes in his environment. Despite these efforts to stay safe, Carlos began to notice a change in himself over the years. He felt more and more disconnected from others – colleagues, friends, even his own students. Simple tasks, like grocery shopping or going out for dinner, had become daunting ordeals. His divorce several years prior had left him feeling isolated, but now he wondered if there was something deeper at play. One day, while teaching a lesson on emotional regulation to a group of rowdy teenagers, Carlos caught himself scanning the room with an unusual level of intensity. He realized that his own fears and avoidance behaviors had been shaping his interactions – not just with his students, but with everyone around him. It was this moment that brought him to seek help, a hesitant acknowledgment that perhaps it was time to confront the memories he'd spent so long avoiding. As Carlos sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands and glancing toward the door, he couldn't shake the feeling of vulnerability. He was most afraid of losing control – not just of his emotions but of his very surroundings. What frightened him most was the possibility that he'd never be able to fully shed the armor he'd built around himself. And yet, as he looked at the therapist with a mix of trepidation and hope, Carlos whispered a quiet admission: maybe it's time to try.
